sources.locator: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2; W3C Recommendation 2023; provisions applicable to Complex-table alternatives
sources.claim: Complex tables should be simplified or split when possible; otherwise explicit header associations and linear reading checks must preserve meaning.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Complex tables — merged cells, headers in several tiers, irregular layouts — are hard for everyone, and especially for screen-reader users. **First, simplify**: split into two tables, repeat a label, or reorganise rows. Only when the structure truly needs it, wire relationships explicitly: give each header an `id` and list the relevant ids in each data cell's `headers` attribute.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A finance report has a header row "2025 | 2026", and under each year "Revenue | Costs". Some cells span two rows, others two columns. Sighted readers squint; screen-reader users get the wrong headers. A two-tier financial header uses unique ids and headers attributes only after a simpler table design is found insufficient. In this lesson you'll review a complex table and propose an accessible structural alternative.

What's the best first move?", "options": ["Add more colspan and rowspan to make it neater", "See if it can be split or reorganised into simpler tables"], "answer": 1, "why": "Every extra merged tier makes the table harder to read and to mark up. Simplify first; wire up ids/headers only if you must."}

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Heading hierarchy** and **Captions and context** — plus th and scope from the headers lesson.

sections.heading: The rule: simplify first, then wire explicitly
sections.body:
**Option A — simplify** (preferred): one table per year, each with columns Quarter, Revenue, Costs. **Option B — explicit wiring**, when one combined table is truly needed: ```html
Revenue and costs by year (₹ lakh)
2025 2026
RevenueCosts RevenueCosts
Q1 4031 5236
``` | Approach | Cost | |---|---| | split tables. | easy to read and maintain. | | scope only. | fine for simple two-way tables. | | ids + headers. | precise but laborious and fragile. | ```reveal {"prompt": "Why are ids + headers fragile?", "answer": "Every data cell lists its header ids by hand. Add a column or reorder rows and many attributes must change — easy to get wrong."} ```

sections.heading: Review questions

includes: Review complex tables and propose simpler structures.
Use id/headers when a multi-tier table can't be simplified.

outcomes: Review a complex table and propose an accessible structural alternative.

examples.title: A two-tier financial header
examples.situation: A two-tier financial header uses unique ids and headers attributes only after a simpler table design is found insufficient.
walkthrough: **Try simpler first:** splitting by year was rejected because the report must compare 2025 and 2026 side by side.
**Unique ids:** each year and each Revenue/Costs header gets its own id (y25, r25, c25…).
**Headers attributes:** each data cell lists its row and both column tiers, e.g. `headers="q1 y26 r26"`; a screen reader will read "Q1, 2026, Revenue, 52".
examples.result: Every value is announced with its quarter, year and measure, and the extra complexity is justified by a real need.

examples.title: The merged-cell monster
examples.situation: A timetable merges rooms, days and time slots across three header tiers with dozens of rowspans.
walkthrough: Screen readers announce wrong or missing headers for many cells.
Even sighted users struggle to trace a cell back to its headers.
Proposal: one table per day, columns Time, Subject, Room — no merged cells at all.
examples.result: Five simple tables replace one monster, and every cell has obvious headers.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: More merged header cells always make a table easier to understand.
misconceptions.correction: Each merged tier adds reading and markup complexity. Simplify first by splitting or relabelling; use explicit id/headers wiring only when a complex structure is truly necessary.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The merged-cell monster", what structure replaced the merged headers?

analogy.example: A complex table is like a **road junction with seven exits**: you can add more signs (headers attributes), but often it's better to build two simple junctions (split tables).
limitations: Roads are expensive to rebuild; tables aren't.
Signs must be updated whenever roads change — like headers attributes.

steps.explanation: A simpler table design is found insufficient for the comparison.
The two-tier financial header uses unique ids.
Each data cell's headers attribute lists all its headers.

nearTransfer.prompt: A table merges "Morning" and "Evening" over three columns each. Propose a simpler structure that avoids the merge.
expectedEvidence: Or two tables, one per session.

farTransfer.prompt: Take a real complex table (a timetable, results sheet or financial report). Write a review with the problems, propose a simpler alternative, and build it.
scaffold: Test the original with a screen reader.

remediation.explanation: Checklist: **Can I split it? Can I repeat labels instead of merging? Is scope enough? Only then: ids + headers.**

recap.summary: To review a complex table and propose an accessible alternative, simplify first — split tables, repeat labels, reorganise rows. Use unique ids and headers attributes only when a multi-tier structure is genuinely needed.
